intro: A lilting dance in 12/8 grows over long bass notes that suggest rustic bagpipes. The refrain’s returns pass through minor keys before the finale regains E major.
question: When the dance returns in a different key, what still makes it recognisable?

sections.mNote: the refrain returns in C♯ minor and moves towards B major

cues.title: A dance over a drone
cues.text: The tune rocks in four groups of three quavers, the 12/8 metre of this pastoral dance. Under it, long E and B notes suggest the fixed drones of bagpipes without adding any bagpipe to the string ensemble.
cues.evidence: Mutopia III, opening 12 bars, shows the compound metre and sustained bass notes. Resonances explains the pastoral drone: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301; https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring.

cues.title: Nymphs and shepherds
cues.text: Spring’s last sonnet stanza imagines nymphs and shepherds dancing to rustic bagpipes. These are conventional figures of the pastoral world, not named characters in a plot that the violin must narrate note by note.
cues.evidence: The final stanza names nymphs, shepherds and bagpipes: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36996.

cues.title: The refrain in a minor key
cues.text: The dance shape returns in C♯ minor. Its familiar rhythm survives the change of key, and the passage continues onwards rather than settling into a simple replay of the opening.
cues.evidence: The same-recording analysis places the second ritornello near 0:58.5; the report’s C♯-minor region extends across about 0:45–1:15. The score has the refrain in C♯ minor at movement bar 22: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More than a concerto composer
cues.text: Vivaldi’s first staged opera, Ottone in villa, was performed in Vicenza in 1713. His career in the theatre ran alongside the instrumental music for which he is now most widely known.
cues.evidence: The Pietà biography identifies Ottone in villa, Vicenza, 1713: https://www.vivaldichurchvenice.com/en/biography-of-antonio-vivaldi.

cues.title: The solo line and its support
cues.text: During this extended episode, compare the solo violin’s changing figures with the longer notes and recurring patterns beneath it. The accompaniment does not have to imitate the soloist’s speed to give its movement direction.
cues.evidence: The score’s extended second solo includes sustained bass support and answering violin figures, followed by repeated quavers; the report is relatively subdued around 1:45–2:15. This prompt covers the episode rather than timing a single answer: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301; https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The same tonic, another mode
cues.text: The returning dance passes from E major to E minor. The tonal centre stays E, but G-sharp gives way to G-natural. Listen for the familiar figure carrying a changed harmonic colour.
cues.evidence: The score changes to E minor at movement bar 61; the same-recording commentary places the mixed major/minor refrain at about 2:29.5–3:04.5. The report marks a strong change at 2:40 and a minor-compatible region later in that span: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Published as a collection
cues.text: The Four Seasons opened Vivaldi’s Op. 8, published in Amsterdam in 1725. The seasonal titles and attached poems invite detailed listening, but the solo episodes also follow the concerto’s musical business of contrast, travel and return.
cues.evidence: The Pietà biography documents the 1725 Amsterdam publication; the movement’s episodes and returns are established in the score: https://www.vivaldichurchvenice.com/en/biography-of-antonio-vivaldi; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

cues.title: The dance finds E major again
cues.text: The last refrain restores E major. Its final phrases include a quieter echo before the ending; listen for a change of level without a change of the dance’s basic pulse.
cues.evidence: The score returns to E major at bar 79 and marks the later phrase piano at bar 86. The guide places the last refrain near 3:32; report levels retreat around 3:50–4:00: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The drone gives way to a travelling bass
transitions.how: The full-string refrain releases the solo violin while the bass begins to move away from its held E and B. Ascending sequences lead through A and B towards C♯ minor; chromatic descending bass motion then intensifies the approach to the next refrain.
transitions.evidence: The score’s first solo starts within bar 12; the guide places it at 0:33.5 and explains the sequence and chromatic bass. Report pitch estimates move from E to C♯ minor shortly afterwards: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: The dance shape returns in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The solo passage reaches C♯ minor and the full strings resume the opening dance figure in that key. Its characteristic rhythm makes the return audible before the continuing sequence moves through E major towards B major.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bar 22 marks tutti in C♯ minor. The guide’s synchronization gives 0:58.5 and its prose explains the later B-major destination; report windows around 0:55–1:15 favour C♯ minor: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: A cadence releases the soloist again
transitions.how: The refrain reaches B major. The soloist begins another mobile episode, with the orchestral violins answering later within it. A chain of fifth-related harmonies takes the line away from B before bringing it back; the 12/8 pulse continues through the handover.
transitions.evidence: The score marks solo in bar 34, after the B-major cadence. The same-recording guide starts this episode at 1:30 and describes its harmonic itinerary: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: The returning tune changes mode
transitions.how: The solo passage ends in B major, and the refrain begins again in E major. Within a few bars its G-sharp changes to G-natural and the music proceeds in E minor. The return therefore supplies both recognition and a new departure.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bars 58–61 show tutti and the change of key signature. The guide gives about 2:29.5 for the return; the analysis report has strong changes at 2:28 and 2:40: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

transitions.title: The strings leave a dominant pedal
transitions.how: The orchestral violins withdraw while the solo violin moves over a sustained B in the bass. The dominant pedal holds the harmony in suspense: the soloist’s changing notes can intensify the phrase without immediately changing its foundation.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia bars 71–78 show orchestral rests and the sustained B bass. The guide gives about 3:04.5; the report marks a change at 3:04: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301; https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php.

transitions.title: Major-mode dance after the held dominant
transitions.how: The long B support resolves towards E and the full-string dance returns in E major. The familiar dotted figure replaces the solo figuration; Vivaldi needs no new tempo to make the final arrival clear.
transitions.evidence: The score restores E major and tutti at bar 79. The guide gives about 3:32 and the report marks 3:30, with renewed E-major-compatible content: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/03.php; https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.

source.title: Vivaldi, The Four Seasons — Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles

timeline.note: Full-string dance over sustained bass notes.
First solo episode; orchestral upper strings rest while the basso supports the violin.
The minor-key refrain restores the full strings.
Extended solo-led passage; upper strings answer and the bass later rests, so this is passage-level participation.
The refrain returns and changes from E major to E minor.
Solo violin over the sustained B bass; orchestral violins rest.
The full-string closing dance regains E major.

facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.
composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
